notes.title: Biology: Mitochondria
notes.text:
Mitochondria are double-membrane structures found in nearly all eukaryotic cells. Their inner membrane is folded into cristae, which increases the surface area available for the electron transport chain. Through oxidative phosphorylation, mitochondria convert nutrients into ATP, the molecule that cells spend to do work.

Mitochondria carry their own circular DNA and divide independently of the cell, which supports the endosymbiotic theory: they descend from free-living bacteria engulfed by an ancestral cell.

notes.title: Biology: Photosynthesis
notes.text:
Photosynthesis takes place in chloroplasts. In the light-dependent reactions, chlorophyll in the thylakoid membranes captures light, splits water molecules and releases oxygen, while producing ATP and NADPH.

The Calvin cycle then runs in the stroma. It uses the ATP and NADPH to fix carbon dioxide into glucose. Because the Calvin cycle does not need light directly, it is also called the light-independent stage.

notes.title: Biology: DNA Replication
notes.text:
DNA replication copies the genome before a cell divides. The enzyme helicase unwinds the double helix at the origin of replication, and each separated strand serves as a template for a new complementary strand.

DNA polymerase builds the new strand only in the 5' to 3' direction, so the lagging strand is made in short Okazaki fragments that ligase later joins. Because each new molecule keeps one original strand, the process is called semiconservative.

notes.title: Biology: Immune System
notes.text:
The immune system has two layers. The innate response is fast and general: barriers such as skin, phagocytes that engulf invaders, and inflammation at the site of injury.

The adaptive response is slower but specific. B cells produce antibodies that bind a particular antigen, while T cells destroy infected cells or coordinate the response. Memory cells remain afterwards, which is why a vaccine can prepare the body for a later infection.

notes.title: Networking: TCP vs UDP
notes.text:
TCP is a connection-oriented transport protocol. It opens a connection with a three-way handshake, numbers every segment, retransmits anything that is lost and delivers data in order, which makes it reliable but slower.

UDP is connectionless. It sends independent datagrams with no handshake, no retransmission and no ordering guarantee. Its low overhead makes it a good fit for live video, online games and DNS lookups, where a late packet is worth less than a missing one.

notes.title: Databases: Normalization
notes.text:
Database normalization organizes tables to reduce redundancy and prevent update anomalies. First normal form requires atomic values, so every column holds a single value. Second normal form removes partial dependencies on part of a composite key.

Third normal form removes transitive dependencies, meaning non-key columns must depend only on the key. Denormalizing on purpose can speed up read-heavy reporting queries at the cost of extra storage.

notes.title: Computer Science: Hash Tables
notes.text:
A hash table stores key-value pairs by running each key through a hash function that picks a bucket. Lookups, inserts and deletes take constant time on average, which makes hash tables the usual choice for dictionaries and caches.

When two keys land in the same bucket, a collision occurs. Chaining keeps a list in each bucket, while open addressing probes for the next free slot. A high load factor makes collisions more frequent, so the table is resized and rehashed.

notes.title: Computer Science: Big-O Notation
notes.text:
Big-O notation describes how the running time or memory of an algorithm grows as the input size grows, ignoring constant factors. Constant time is O(1), binary search is O(log n), scanning a list is O(n) and simple nested loops are O(n squared).

It describes the worst case unless stated otherwise. Two algorithms with the same Big-O can still differ in practice, but the notation shows which one will fall behind first when the data becomes large.

notes.title: Software: Git Basics
notes.text:
Git is a distributed version control system. A commit records a snapshot of the project, and a branch is a movable pointer to a line of commits, so work on a new feature can happen without touching the main line.

A merge combines two branches, and a conflict appears when both changed the same lines. Rebase replays commits on top of another branch for a linear history. Push and pull exchange commits with a remote repository.

notes.title: History: French Revolution
notes.text:
The French Revolution began in 1789 when the Estates-General met and the Third Estate declared itself a National Assembly. On 14 July the Bastille prison was stormed, and in August the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen was adopted.

The monarchy ended with the execution of Louis XVI in 1793. The Reign of Terror followed under Robespierre and the Committee of Public Safety, and the decade closed with Napoleon Bonaparte seizing power in 1799.

notes.title: History: Industrial Revolution
notes.text:
The Industrial Revolution began in Britain in the late 1700s. Steam engines, powered by coal, drove factories and railways, and mechanized spinning and weaving moved textile production from homes into mills.

Cities grew quickly as workers left farms, bringing crowded housing, long hours and child labor. Over time these conditions led to factory laws and the rise of trade unions, while productivity and living standards slowly increased.

notes.title: History: Cold War
notes.text:
The Cold War was a long rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union after 1945. Direct war was avoided, and the conflict played out through an arms race, spying, propaganda and proxy wars in Korea and Vietnam.

The Berlin Wall divided a city from 1961 and became its symbol, and the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 brought the powers close to nuclear war. The Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, which ended the confrontation.

notes.title: Economics: Inflation
notes.text:
Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, which reduces the purchasing power of money. It is usually measured by the consumer price index, which tracks the cost of a fixed basket of goods and services over time.

Demand-pull inflation happens when spending outpaces supply, while cost-push inflation comes from higher input costs such as wages or energy. Central banks typically respond by raising interest rates to cool demand.

notes.title: Economics: Supply and Demand
notes.text:
In a market, price rises when buyers want more of a good than sellers offer, and falls when sellers offer more than buyers want. The equilibrium price is where the quantity supplied equals the quantity demanded.

A shift in demand, such as a change in income or taste, moves the curve and sets a new equilibrium. Elasticity measures how strongly quantity reacts to a price change: necessities tend to be inelastic and luxuries elastic.

notes.title: Physics: Newton's Laws
notes.text:
Newton's first law says an object keeps its state of rest or uniform motion unless a net force acts on it. The second law states that acceleration equals net force divided by mass, so the same force moves a lighter object faster.

The third law says that when one body pushes on another, the second pushes back with an equal and opposite force. A rocket moves forward because it throws exhaust backward.

notes.title: Physics: Thermodynamics
notes.text:
The first law of thermodynamics says energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted: the change in internal energy equals heat added minus work done by the system.

The second law says that the entropy of an isolated system never decreases, which is why heat flows from hot to cold by itself and why no engine can turn heat completely into work. Absolute zero is the lowest possible temperature.

notes.title: Psychology: Classical Conditioning
notes.text:
Classical conditioning, studied by Ivan Pavlov, is learning by association. A neutral stimulus, such as a bell, is repeatedly paired with an unconditioned stimulus, such as food, that naturally causes a response.

After enough pairings the bell alone triggers salivation, and it becomes a conditioned stimulus. If the bell is later presented without food, the response gradually fades, which is called extinction.

notes.title: Chemistry: Acids and Bases
notes.text:
An acid donates hydrogen ions in water and a base accepts them. The pH scale runs from 0 to 14: values below 7 are acidic, 7 is neutral and values above 7 are basic, with each step representing a tenfold change in hydrogen ion concentration.

When an acid reacts with a base, they neutralize each other and form water and a salt. A buffer is a solution that resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added.
